live.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
live.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT: a threat actor known by many names
live.in_short: The catalogue lists NICKEL FOXCROFT under many aliases, including APT37 and ScarCruft, and names eight tools tied to it. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL FOXCROFT is the Secureworks name for a threat actor tracked under many other names.
Its aliases include APT37, ATK4, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Operation Daybreak, Operaton Erebus, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA, Reaper, ScarCruft, TA-RedAnt and Venus 121.
The catalogue links eight tools to the actor: Bluelight, Chinotto, GOLDBACKDOOR, KevDroid, KoSpy, PoorWeb, ROKRAT and final1stpy.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL FOXCROFT
next.headline: NICKEL FOXCROFT (APT37, ScarCruft): a long-running espionage group focused on South Korea
next.in_short: NICKEL FOXCROFT, also tracked as APT37 and ScarCruft, is described by vendors as a North Korea-linked espionage actor. Reports cover Android spyware and an air-gap USB campaign.

sentences.t: NICKEL FOXCROFT is tracked by Secureworks. Its catalogue aliases include APT37, ScarCruft, Group 123, InkySquid, Moldy Pisces, Reaper, RICOCHET CHOLLIMA and Venus 121.
CrowdStrike calls RICOCHET CHOLLIMA a DPRK-nexus targeted intrusion adversary. It says the group has been involved in espionage since at least 2016.
Lookout describes ScarCruft as a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage group active since 2012.
CrowdStrike says the group's observed operations have almost exclusively targeted the Republic of Korea.
CrowdStrike assesses the focus is on South Korean government officials, NGOs, academics and journalists. Its page text is truncated, so the profile is incomplete.
Lookout says the group has also operated in Japan, Vietnam, Russia, Nepal, China, India and Romania, among other countries.
Zscaler ThreatLabz says APT37 has abused malicious shortcut (LNK) files as an initial vector for years.
Lookout describes KoSpy as Android spyware that uses fake utility app lures. It records keystrokes by abusing accessibility services.
Lookout says KoSpy uses a two-stage approach to managing its command servers. It says this gives the operator flexibility and resilience.
Zscaler says the Ruby Jumper toolkit uses removable media to reach air-gapped networks. It includes a backdoor called THUMBSBD and a tool called VIRUSTASK.
Lookout reports KoSpy samples dated from March 2022 to March 2024. They posed as five different apps, distributed via Google Play and Firebase Firestore.
Lookout attributes KoSpy to APT37 with medium confidence. It also notes ties to infrastructure used by APT43, another North Korean group.
Lookout says the apps were removed from Google Play and the Firebase projects were deactivated.

Zscaler ThreatLabz published a report on 2026-02-26 about APT37's Ruby Jumper campaign. The chain starts with an LNK file and delivers RESTLEAF, then SNAKEDROPPER, which installs a backdoored Ruby runtime.
Zscaler says that, to its knowledge, this is the first time APT37 has abused Zoho WorkDrive. RESTLEAF uses it for command and control.
Zscaler says THUMBSBD also delivers BLUELIGHT, a previously documented backdoor.
Treat unexpected shortcut files and USB media with caution, and install apps only from sources you trust.
